source_metadata.title: High-dose intravenous vitamin C, a promising multi-targeting agent in the treatment of cancer
source_metadata.journal: Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research
source_metadata.design: narrative review with targeted literature searches for selected preclinical and clinical subsets
source_metadata.source_scope_warning: This review summarizes heterogeneous preclinical and clinical literature. Results from cited studies are secondary reports and should be checked in the primary publications before reuse as primary evidence.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review aims to provide an up-to-date overview of high-dose vitamin C in cancer therapy, covering preclinical and clinical monotherapy and combination studies, proposed molecular mechanisms, global molecular profiling, research gaps, and future clinical implications.

The review distinguishes oral vitamin C, which it reports reaches plasma concentrations no higher than 220 micromol/L, from pharmacological intravenous vitamin C, which it reports can produce plasma concentrations of at least 15 mmol/L.
The authors frame millimolar vitamin C concentrations as the exposure range required for cancer-cell killing in the preclinical studies they summarize.
The abstract states that strong clinical data and phase III studies are lacking despite the preclinical and early clinical literature on high-dose intravenous vitamin C in cancer.

The authors report that F.B., A.V.M. and L.C. performed the literature searches, but the article does not describe a single systematic-review protocol, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or certainty-of-evidence framework for the review as a whole.

The review summarizes phase I and a few phase II studies as showing high tolerability and safety with signals of efficacy, while also presenting high-dose intravenous vitamin C as a possible means to reduce treatment toxicity and improve quality of life.
The review reports preclinical anticancer activity of vitamin C at approximately 1 to 20 mM across multiple tumor models.
The review reports that high-dose intravenous vitamin C monotherapy in advanced malignancies was administered at doses up to 3 g/kg without significant toxicity in the cited phase I literature.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: maximum reported IVC dose without significant toxicity

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports a maximum achievable plasma ascorbate concentration of 49 mM in the cited high-dose intravenous vitamin C monotherapy studies.

The review reports that grade 3 or higher adverse events possibly related to intravenous vitamin C occurred in only 1 to 2 participants per cited monotherapy study of 17 to 24 participants, with hypokalemia, hypernatremia, hypertension and anemia among the reported events.
The review states that no objective antitumor response was observed in the cited high-dose intravenous vitamin C monotherapy studies.
The review reports stable disease in 3 of 16 evaluable patients in the Stephenson high-dose intravenous vitamin C monotherapy study.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review notes that the Nielsen monotherapy study used a maximum whole-body dose of 60 g once weekly for 12 weeks and observed no disease remission or stabilization, then interprets dose and administration frequency as possible contributors to the result.

The review notes that high-dose vitamin C monotherapy has generally been assessed in terminally ill or heavily pretreated patients, which the authors identify as a possible reason for limited clinical response and as a constraint on evaluating monotherapy in less heavily treated patients.

From the monotherapy literature, the authors identify studies using intravenous vitamin C at least three times per week as the studies they considered to warrant further trials and cite recommended doses ranging from 1.5 g/kg to 1.9 to 2.2 g/kg.

The review describes retrospective and observational palliative-care studies that reported improvements in symptoms or quality of life after intravenous vitamin C, including appetite, fatigue, depression, sleep disturbance, nausea, tumor pain and loss of appetite.

source_anchor.paragraph: VitC monotherapy in palliative care and quality of life

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports a retrospective study of radiotherapy-resistant bone metastases in which median survival was 10 months with intravenous vitamin C and 2 months in the comparison group.

source_anchor.paragraph: VitC monotherapy in palliative care and quality of life

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors conclude that the most plausible future role for high-dose intravenous vitamin C as cancer therapy is in combination strategies rather than as monotherapy.

The review maps 71 preclinical combination studies published from 1989 through 2021 and describes 59 anticancer agents or combinations used with high-dose vitamin C; Table 1 focuses on 44 preclinical studies from 2016 through 2021.

The review reports that Schoenfeld and colleagues observed an approximately 50 percent increase in overall survival in NSCLC and glioblastoma mouse models when pharmacological ascorbate was added to carboplatin and radiation.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review highlights a glioblastoma experiment in which lower-dose ascorbate with a single nonstandard radiation fraction was associated with faster tumor progression than radiation alone, illustrating that dose and treatment schedule can alter the direction of a preclinical combination effect.

atoms.canonical_statement: For the clinical combination section, the authors report a PubMed search using ascorbate or vitamin C together with cancer and clinical trial, which identified 34 completed studies; 16 used medium-to-high dose intravenous vitamin C and 4 of those 16 were monotherapy studies.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review states that most published clinical studies were small and that no large-scale double-blind randomized trial of high-dose intravenous vitamin C in cancer had been completed at the time of publication.

source_anchor.paragraph: Clinical studies combining chemotherapy and radiation therapy

atoms.canonical_statement: Across the combination studies, the review states that grade 3 or higher adverse events were generally attributed by the cited investigators to the underlying cancer or standard anticancer therapy rather than to intravenous vitamin C.

The authors note that low accrual and changes in standard cancer therapy led to termination or poor recruitment in several trials, limiting the clinical evidence base for specific high-dose vitamin C combinations.

The authors characterize the clinical combination data as favorable efficacy trends rather than definitive efficacy evidence because the published studies were generally too small to establish treatment benefit.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review identifies 14 described mechanistic effects across recent vitamin C combination studies and notes that 7 effects were reported more than six times.
The review presents hydrogen-peroxide-dependent pro-oxidant activity as the most widely described cancer-selective mechanism of pharmacological vitamin C.

The review describes a concentration-dependent redox pattern in which approximately 30 to 80 micromolar vitamin C is mainly antioxidant, whereas pharmacological concentrations around 0.5 to 20 mM can act as a pro-oxidant and increase reactive oxygen species.

The review describes GLUT1-mediated uptake of dehydroascorbic acid and its intracellular reduction as a mechanism that can consume glutathione and NADPH, weaken antioxidant defenses, and amplify oxidative stress in susceptible cancer cells.
The review describes vitamin C as a cofactor for enzymes involved in collagen synthesis, HIF regulation and TET-dependent DNA demethylation.
The review links vitamin C-supported collagen synthesis and extracellular matrix remodeling with reduced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, invasion and metastatic behavior in preclinical models.
The review describes vitamin C-supported HIF hydroxylase activity as a route to HIF-1 degradation and reduced hypoxia signaling.
The review describes restoration or activation of TET enzyme activity by vitamin C as a mechanism for DNA demethylation and re-expression of tumor suppressor programs.
The review reports preclinical AML work in which combining an IDH1 inhibitor with high-dose vitamin C increased TET activity, reduced cell growth and promoted differentiation.

The review reports preclinical synergy between high-dose vitamin C and PD-1 or CTLA-4 immune checkpoint blockade and notes a stronger effect in immunocompetent than immunocompromised mice in one cited study.

The mechanistic evidence summarized by the review is dominated by preclinical cell and animal studies, so the described mechanisms do not by themselves establish clinical efficacy or patient-selection rules.
The review identifies a limited set of global molecular profiling studies of vitamin C in cancer, largely in cell-line models and using proteomic, transcriptomic or metabolomic methods.

source_anchor.paragraph: Global molecular profiling studies on high-dose IVC in cancer context

atoms.canonical_statement: Across the proteomic studies, the review highlights recurrent changes in glycolysis, iron metabolism, cell-cycle regulation and protein translation after vitamin C exposure.
The review notes that most transcriptomic studies used vitamin C concentrations below 1 mM, which limits how directly those results apply to pharmacological high-dose intravenous exposure.

The transcriptomic studies summarized by the review implicate apoptosis, extracellular matrix remodeling, iron metabolism, glycolysis, DNA replication and mismatch-repair programs in cellular responses to vitamin C.
The review identifies four metabolomic studies in breast, colorectal and hepatocellular cancer models and states that all four reported reduced ATP and NAD after high-dose vitamin C.

The metabolomic studies summarized by the review showed accumulation of glycolytic metabolites upstream of GAPDH with depletion of downstream metabolites, a pattern the authors interpret as consistent with GAPDH inhibition and disruption of glycolysis and the TCA cycle.

The authors conclude that global profiling studies support redox and metabolic mechanisms already described in targeted studies while also pointing to cytoskeletal remodeling, translation inhibition and DNA replication or repair as additional processes that merit study.

The authors propose KRAS-mutant tumors, TET2- or IDH1-mutant disease, tumors with a high labile iron pool or low ferroportin, mismatch-repair-deficient tumors, and selected immune-checkpoint contexts as hypotheses for groups that may be especially sensitive to high-dose vitamin C.
The review states that no phase III clinical trial of high-dose intravenous vitamin C in cancer had been completed at the time of the 2021 publication.

The review describes ongoing phase III programs, including a Chinese colorectal cancer study of 1.5 g/kg intravenous vitamin C with FOLFOX with or without bevacizumab; the status is reported as of the review period and was not externally updated in this extraction.

The authors advise screening for renal insufficiency and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency before high-dose intravenous vitamin C because they associate these conditions with oxalate nephropathy or kidney stones and hemolytic anemia, respectively.

Based on the studies reviewed, the authors favor intravenous dosing sufficient to reach millimolar plasma concentrations, cite monotherapy doses of 1.5 to 1.9 to 2.2 g/kg and combination doses around 75 to 87.5 g, and favor administration at least twice weekly, commonly two to three times weekly for at least 8 weeks.

The authors conclude that further clinical testing of high-dose intravenous vitamin C is needed before its proposed cancer-selective, treatment-sensitizing and toxicity-reducing effects can be established for routine cancer treatment.

extraction_limitations: The source is a narrative review rather than a primary empirical study.
Results from cited studies are represented as secondary reports and tagged secondary_reported_result where applicable.
The review does not provide a single systematic-review protocol, formal study-level risk-of-bias assessment, or certainty-of-evidence framework for the review as a whole.
The 265-entry bibliography was not atomized. It was exported to a separate Markdown task queue.
All model-extracted atoms remain needs_review because no independent human source-verification step is represented.
No external current-practice or trial-status verification was performed because @VERIFY was not activated.
schema_gaps: The LiteratureAtom schema is oriented toward primary literature and has no dedicated atom kind for a narrative review synthesis or secondary reported study result. These assertions use existing kinds plus review_article and secondary_reported_result tags.
Clinical recommendation-like statements in the review are author conclusions, not guideline recommendations, and are tagged not_current_guidance where appropriate.
